items.question:
An audit team at a professional services firm has used the same Claude Project for three years across multiple client engagements. Documents from concluded engagements — including client financial models, board presentations, and legal due-diligence memos — were added over time but never removed. A new team member joins and uses the Project for a current engagement, unaware of its contents.

What is the PRIMARY risk from the accumulated stale documents in the Project?

options.A: Prior client confidential data stored in the knowledge base is available to Claude in every session, meaning it could surface in work for current clients without anyone intending a disclosure
options.B: Stale documents will cause Claude to produce outdated analysis since the model always prioritises knowledge-base documents over its training data
options.C: The Project knowledge base will become too large to process efficiently once it contains three years of documents
options.D: The prior clients may be entitled to access the Project under data subject access rights since their data is stored there

items.question:
A senior IT manager at a government ministry is deploying a Claude API integration to process citizen benefit application data. The AI vendor's sales team verbally confirms in a meeting that 'data stays in your region.' No specific contractual term or technical routing configuration is established. The ministry's policy requires that all citizen data be processed on domestic infrastructure.

Why is the verbal assurance insufficient as a data-residency control?

options.A: Verbal assurances from sales teams are inadmissible in regulatory proceedings only if they were not recorded
options.B: Data-residency obligations require enforceable contractual commitments and technical routing controls — verbal assurances create no legally binding obligation and cannot be audited or enforced
options.C: The vendor's sales team may be unaware of the ministry's specific regulatory requirements, so the assurance was likely given in good faith and is enforceable as a pre-contractual statement
options.D: Verbal assurances are sufficient if the ministry follows up with a written confirmation email within 30 days

items.question:
A UK-based insurance company configures its enterprise Claude API to use a US endpoint as the default, suitable for its US team. A UK team member uses the same account to process EU policyholder data — names, addresses, and health-related claim histories — believing the company's enterprise agreement resolves all cross-border issues. Legal counsel reviews the configuration and flags a concern.

What specific gap is legal counsel MOST likely identifying?

options.A: The US team's API calls are now co-mingled with the UK team's calls, creating a data contamination risk
options.B: The enterprise agreement covers the US endpoint adequately; legal counsel's concern is likely about the health claim data qualifying as special-category data
options.C: EU policyholder health data routed to a US endpoint constitutes a cross-border transfer of special-category data; the enterprise agreement alone does not establish a valid transfer mechanism for this specific flow
options.D: The UK team member should have used the US team's account rather than creating a separate transfer by using the UK-configured account

items.question:
A document review specialist at a life sciences company used a Claude Project to support a regulatory submission three years ago. The project's documents — including patient clinical trial data, internal safety analyses, and regulatory correspondence — were subject to a 3-year post-submission retention schedule. The submission date has now passed. The Project and its full contents remain active and accessible to the entire regulatory affairs team.

What is the PRIMARY compliance concern?

options.A: The regulatory agency may audit the company and request copies of the data, so it should be retained beyond the schedule as a precaution
options.B: The clinical trial data may now be outdated and could mislead future regulatory submissions if accessed
options.C: The team members who have left the company may still be able to access the Project since their access was never revoked
options.D: Retaining personal and sensitive clinical data beyond the defined retention schedule constitutes unnecessary processing with no valid legal basis, creating regulatory exposure

items.question:
A nurse informatics specialist at a teaching hospital discovers that a colleague accidentally submitted a spreadsheet of 200 patient discharge summaries — containing patient names, diagnoses, and readmission dates — to a personal Claude.ai account rather than the hospital's enterprise API account with a signed BAA. The submission happened 20 minutes ago. The colleague has closed the browser tab.

What should the specialist do FIRST?

options.A: Document what was submitted — the data category, approximate volume, timestamp, and account type — and immediately notify the hospital's privacy officer to initiate a breach-risk assessment
options.B: Log in to the colleague's personal account and delete the conversation containing the patient data
options.C: Instruct the colleague to submit the same file through the correct enterprise account to restore the properly protected version
options.D: Wait 24 hours to see whether the vendor notifies the hospital of any issue before escalating internally

items.question:
A management consultant at a 50-person advisory firm uploads a client-facing pitch deck to Claude for feedback on structure and narrative. The PowerPoint file was created internally and contains tracked changes showing disagreements between partners, comments with employee names attributed, and document properties listing the firm's internal project code and client name in the metadata.

What data risk does uploading the source file MOST directly create?

options.A: The pitch deck's visual design elements may be reproduced by Claude and used in competing proposals
options.B: Document metadata — tracked changes, author names, comments, and file properties — may contain confidential and personal information not visible in the rendered presentation but accessible when the file is processed
options.C: Uploading a file larger than 10MB will cause the model to truncate the analysis
options.D: The client name in the file properties constitutes PII and triggers a data-processing agreement requirement

items.question:
An enterprise Claude API customer in the healthcare sector learns during contract review that Anthropic uses third-party cloud infrastructure providers for compute. The DPA in place covers Anthropic's handling of PHI. A healthcare compliance attorney reviews the arrangement and identifies two concerns that the current DPA should address but may not.

Which TWO provisions should the compliance attorney MOST likely require in a strengthened DPA? (Choose TWO)

options.A: A clause requiring the healthcare organisation to indemnify Anthropic for any breach caused by the cloud infrastructure provider
options.B: A provision requiring Anthropic to flow down equivalent PHI-handling obligations to any subprocessors (including cloud infrastructure providers) it engages
options.C: A notification obligation requiring Anthropic to inform the healthcare organisation before engaging a new subprocessor or making material changes to existing subprocessor arrangements
options.D: A clause confirming that cloud infrastructure providers are not business associates since they access only encrypted data at rest
options.E: A requirement that the healthcare organisation pre-approve every individual Anthropic employee who has access to its data

items.question:
An employee wellbeing manager at a large energy company has collected 18 months of weekly self-assessment data from 800 employees through a voluntary mental health support app. The data includes named employees' stress scores, sleep quality ratings, and free-text 'how are you feeling' entries. She plans to use Claude to generate a trends report.

What is the PRIMARY data handling consideration before she proceeds?

options.A: The data cannot be used for trend analysis because it was collected for individual support, not organisational reporting
options.B: Stress and sleep data are financial wellbeing indicators that fall under workplace health-and-safety reporting requirements
options.C: Named employee mental health self-assessments are individually identifiable health-related data — their inclusion in a Claude workflow requires appropriate data-handling controls regardless of the account tier
options.D: The data is suitable for processing on a personal Claude account since it was collected voluntarily and employees consented to the app's terms

items.question:
A senior quantitative analyst at an investment bank runs a time-sensitive portfolio stress-test analysis. Frustrated by the approval queue for the bank's enterprise Claude account, she accesses a direct Anthropic consumer API using a personal credit card and processes 18 months of client portfolio positions — including client names, holding sizes, and currency exposures — to meet a regulatory deadline.

Which of the following MOST accurately characterises the primary governance failure?

options.A: The analyst used a paid consumer API, which is technically an enterprise-class service and therefore adequate for client financial data
options.B: The regulatory deadline justifies the departure from the approved account since the outputs were used for a legitimate compliance purpose
options.C: The primary failure is using a model tier lower than the bank's enterprise deployment, reducing the accuracy of the stress-test analysis
options.D: Accessing the API on a personal account bypasses the bank's DPA, audit logging, and access controls — all of which are required for handling client financial data regardless of deadline pressure

items.question:
A data analyst at a retail company prepares a customer dataset for a Claude-assisted churn analysis. She removes customer names from the export but retains email addresses (formatted as firstname.lastname@domain.com), customer IDs, purchase history, and last-login dates. She considers the dataset appropriately de-identified since 'no names are included.'

What error has the analyst made?

options.A: Email addresses in firstname.lastname format directly encode the customer's name — retaining them while removing names is not meaningful de-identification
options.B: Customer IDs are stronger identifiers than email addresses and should have been removed first
options.C: Last-login dates constitute a sensitive time-based identifier that enables timestamp attacks on the dataset
options.D: Purchase history is the primary PII risk in this dataset because it reveals buying patterns and lifestyle data

items.question:
A retailer's enterprise Claude API account is covered by a DPA specifying customer transaction data processing for fraud detection. The marketing analytics team wants to use the same account to analyse customer survey responses for brand sentiment analysis without informing the legal team. A data governance officer flags the proposal.

Which TWO concerns should the governance officer require the marketing team to address before proceeding? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Amend or extend the DPA to include customer survey data and sentiment analysis as an explicitly covered purpose
options.B: Obtain Anthropic's verbal assurance that survey data can be added to the account scope
options.C: Assess and document the legal basis for processing customer survey data for sentiment analysis, separately from the fraud-detection legal basis
options.D: Upgrade the account to a higher model tier to ensure sentiment analysis accuracy meets marketing standards
options.E: Archive all prior fraud-detection sessions before the account is used for marketing to prevent data contamination

items.question:
An IT security director at a 2,000-person insurance company insists that all personal fields be removed from IT incident-ticket data before the dataset is submitted to Claude for anomaly detection and incident-pattern analysis. The resulting anonymised dataset contains only: ticket category, severity level, resolution time, and a timestamp. After analysis, the team cannot determine which business units have the highest incident rates, whether incidents are concentrated among a specific user population, or whether vendor-managed systems are underperforming.

What data governance principle has been misapplied in this scenario?

options.A: Purpose limitation — removing personal data prevents the analysis from fulfilling its intended compliance purpose
options.B: Data minimisation — the principle requires removing data NOT necessary for the task, not removing ALL personal data regardless of analytical necessity
options.C: Data accuracy — over-anonymised datasets produce inaccurate analysis results
options.D: Accountability — the security director lacks the authority to make anonymisation decisions without board approval

items.question:
A customer success team at a 300-person SaaS company has been using a shared Claude Project for 18 months. Team members have progressively added documents including: customer contracts with named contacts, a spreadsheet of customer renewal probabilities with account sizes, a list of churned customers with exit interview summaries, and internal performance data for individual account managers. No one has reviewed or curated the knowledge base since it was created.

What is the MOST accurate description of the governance risk this situation creates?

options.A: The knowledge base has become too large to retrieve accurate results, degrading the team's analysis quality
options.B: Customer contracts in the knowledge base may be outdated, leading to incorrect renewal advice
options.C: The team may have lost track of a specific document and will be unable to respond to a data subject access request for a customer's personal information
options.D: An unmanaged, growing knowledge base has become an uncontrolled store of customer PII, commercially sensitive data, and employee performance data — without access review, retention management, or documentation of what it contains

items.question:
A hospital analytics team runs two separate Claude queries against pseudonymised patient data. Query 1 returns: 'Patient-3847 was admitted to the Oncology unit on Tuesday and received targeted immunotherapy.' Query 2 — run by a different analyst — returns: 'The full name associated with Patient-3847 is Marcus Webb.' A team lead combines both outputs into a single departmental report.

Which TWO statements MOST accurately characterise the privacy implications of this sequence? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The sequence is compliant because each individual query was run against pseudonymised data
options.B: The combined report constitutes PHI because it directly links an individual's identity to a clinical condition and treatment — a linkage that neither query created independently
options.C: Query 2 was inappropriate because it should never be possible to retrieve the real name associated with a pseudonymised identifier
options.D: The team lead's act of combining the two outputs into a single document re-identified a pseudonymised individual, creating a new document that requires PHI-level handling controls
options.E: The pseudonymisation of Patient-3847 across both queries ensures the combined output remains non-PHI since the token was consistently applied

items.question:
A clinical director at a hospital creates a Claude Project and loads it with 150 anonymised-but-detailed patient case summaries to support department review meetings. She shares the Project with all 25 members of her department, including three medical secretaries, two administrative coordinators, and a facilities liaison who coordinates room bookings for the meetings. The case summaries contain diagnosis, treatment, and outcome narratives.

What data governance principle is MOST directly violated by this sharing configuration?

options.A: Purpose limitation — case summaries collected for clinical review cannot be shared with administrative staff
options.B: Data accuracy — sharing case summaries with non-clinical staff increases the risk that the data will be misinterpreted and inaccurately documented
options.C: Minimum necessary access — non-clinical administrative staff have no need to access patient case summaries; sharing the Project with them grants access beyond what their role requires
options.D: Retention — administrative staff should not have access to clinical data past the date of the meeting for which it was shared

items.question:
A constituent services coordinator at a non-profit uses her personal Claude.ai account to summarise 300 supporter emails. Each email contains the supporter's full name, postal address, donation history, and the policy concerns they expressed. She needs to identify common themes in the policy concerns.

What combined action BEST addresses the data governance requirements of this task?

options.A: Switch to an enterprise account, which resolves all data handling concerns for the task
options.B: Anonymise the emails by removing names and addresses before submitting them to the personal account
options.C: Extract only the policy concern text into a separate file and process that file using the personal account
options.D: Process only the policy concern text (stripping names, addresses, and donation data) using the organisation's enterprise account, satisfying both minimisation and contractual data-handling requirements

items.question:
A strategy consulting firm has been engaged by a regional hospital to redesign patient intake and discharge workflows. The hospital's operations team shares a file of 600 actual patient records — names, diagnoses, admission timestamps, and discharge delays — with the lead consultant so she can 'understand what a real case looks like' before modelling the process. The consultant opens the file in Claude via the consulting firm's enterprise account.

What is the PRIMARY compliance concern with this scenario?

options.A: The consulting firm is acting as a business associate by receiving PHI from a covered entity; this requires a BAA between the hospital and the consulting firm before any patient data is shared
options.B: The consulting firm's enterprise account has a DPA, which is equivalent to a BAA and satisfies the hospital's HIPAA obligations
options.C: The consultant should anonymise the patient records herself before opening them in Claude, which resolves the BAA requirement
options.D: Strategy consultants are exempt from BAA requirements since they provide business advice rather than clinical services

items.question:
An EU-based HR manager at a multinational retailer needs to use Claude to analyse European employee pay equity data. The Claude API routes calls to a US data centre. Before submitting, the HR manager removes employee names and replaces them with sequential codes. She considers the submission ready since the names have been redacted.

What additional governance requirement has the HR manager overlooked?

options.A: The sequential codes are quasi-identifiers that could be used to re-identify employees from the HR database
options.B: Pseudonymised employee data is still personal data under GDPR-style frameworks — its transfer to a US data centre requires a valid cross-border transfer mechanism, regardless of identifier removal
options.C: Pay equity data constitutes financial data requiring a separate PCI-compliant workflow
options.D: EU employment data cannot be processed by any AI system without Works Council consultation in all member states

items.question:
A management consultant correctly deletes all client documents from a Claude Project when an engagement closes, fulfilling her firm's document-retention obligations. The Project's system prompt, however, contains detailed instructions referencing the client's internal departmental names, proprietary process terminology, and the client's undisclosed acquisition strategy. The consultant retains the system prompt to reuse its structural elements for a future engagement.

What is the PRIMARY governance concern the consultant has missed?

options.A: Deleting client documents satisfies all post-engagement obligations; system prompts are not documents and are therefore not covered by retention or confidentiality requirements
options.B: The system prompt may trigger Claude to surface the prior client's acquisition strategy in a future engagement by referencing the terminology
options.C: Client-specific confidential information embedded in a system prompt — proprietary terminology, departmental names, undisclosed strategy — is client confidential material subject to the same post-engagement deletion obligation as other documents
options.D: System prompts are stored by Anthropic and may be returned to the client under a data subject access request

items.question:
An insurance company collects detailed personal data from applicants during underwriting — including health status, lifestyle habits, and household composition — under the stated purpose of risk assessment. A data science team plans to run two Claude analyses using this dataset: (1) refine the risk-scoring algorithm, and (2) identify high-net-worth policyholders for targeted wealth management product cross-selling.

Which TWO governance concerns apply to the proposed uses of this dataset? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Using underwriting data to identify cross-sell targets for wealth products constitutes a materially different purpose from risk assessment, requiring a new legal basis
options.B: Any use of health data for insurance purposes is automatically prohibited under privacy frameworks
options.C: The dataset cannot be submitted to Claude in any form since it contains special-category health data
options.D: Submitting the full personal dataset to refine the risk-scoring algorithm may exceed the minimum data necessary for that specific modelling task — only the relevant actuarial fields should be included
options.E: The company must obtain a court order before processing health data for actuarial purposes

items.question:
A customer service agent at an online clothing retailer receives a chat message from a customer that includes the customer's full 16-digit credit card number, pasted by mistake when attempting to share an order number. The agent copies the entire chat log — including the card number — into a personal Claude.ai account to help draft a response addressing the customer's query about a delayed shipment.

What is the PRIMARY compliance violation created by this action?

options.A: The agent read a credit card number that is not part of their job role, violating need-to-know access principles
options.B: Pasting a full payment card number into a personal Claude account processes PCI-regulated data through an uncertified, contractually unprotected channel
options.C: The customer did not consent to their chat data being used to draft a response via an AI tool
options.D: The response should have been drafted using a phone call, not a written channel, to avoid creating a written record of the card number

items.question:
A regional paediatric hospital implements a Claude API integration for clinical documentation. A signed BAA is in place. The IT team, for deployment convenience, grants all 800 clinical and administrative staff access to the integrated workflow — which includes context from patient records across all 12 paediatric wards. A privacy officer reviews the deployment and flags it as non-compliant despite the BAA.

What is the MOST likely basis for the privacy officer's concern?

options.A: The BAA is invalid because it covers too many users — enterprise BAAs should specify a maximum user count
options.B: The integration should have been built using a higher model tier to ensure clinical accuracy, which requires a separately negotiated BAA
options.C: A BAA satisfies the vendor-relationship obligation but does not substitute for implementing minimum-necessary access controls — all 800 staff should not have access to patient records across all wards regardless of the BAA
options.D: The BAA is sufficient provided the hospital obtains patient consent for each clinical documentation session

items.question:
A telemedicine startup processes patient consultation notes through the Claude API to generate personalised follow-up care summaries. A BAA is in place with Anthropic. The patient-facing terms of service include: 'We may use your consultation information to improve and personalise our services.' The startup's product team argues that the BAA + patient ToS consent covers all PHI processing obligations.

What is the MOST significant gap in this reasoning?

options.A: The BAA should have been signed with the patient, not with the AI vendor
options.B: Telemedicine platforms are not covered entities and therefore cannot enter into BAAs
options.C: ToS consent bundled with service acceptance is not explicit consent as required for health data — a separate, specific consent mechanism is needed for each sensitive processing purpose
options.D: The BAA governs the vendor's obligations and the ToS governs one processing purpose; neither establishes a lawful basis for using PHI to 'improve services' — an additional legal basis must be established for that specific purpose beyond what the BAA or acceptance of ToS provides

items.question:
A people analytics lead at a 300-person technology firm removes employee names from a compensation dataset before submitting it to Claude for a pay equity analysis. The remaining fields include job title, department, office location, and salary. One row contains the title 'Chief Information Security Officer, APAC' — a role held by a single person globally.

What redaction error has occurred?

options.A: A job title that only one person holds is functionally equivalent to a direct identifier — it should have been generalised or removed along with the employee's name
options.B: Salary data is a special-category attribute requiring full removal regardless of other redaction steps
options.C: Department and office location together constitute a re-identification risk but are not the primary error in this scenario
options.D: The name was the only field requiring redaction — all other fields are non-personal organisational metadata

items.question:
A hospital analyst realises she has inadvertently created a PHI document by combining two separately pseudonymised Claude query outputs. The resulting document links a specific patient name to an oncology diagnosis and treatment details. She has already shared the document with four colleagues over email. The incident occurred within the past two hours.

What should the analyst do IMMEDIATELY as her first action?

options.A: Email the four colleagues and ask them to delete the document from their inboxes
options.B: Document the details of what happened — what data was combined, when, how many recipients, by which channel — and notify the hospital's privacy officer to initiate the incident response process
options.C: Re-pseudonymise the data in the combined document and redistribute a corrected version to replace the original
options.D: Contact Anthropic's support team to request deletion of the original queries from the model's logs

items.question:
A mental health app company processes anonymised user mood logs through Claude and sells aggregate weekly insights (e.g., 'stress levels rose 18% among users in the 25–34 age bracket this week') to pharmaceutical company clients for market research. The company's DPA with Anthropic covers processing of user mood data. The company argues the derived aggregate outputs are not personal data and can be shared freely.

What is the PRIMARY concern with this practice?

options.A: The pharmaceutical companies receiving the insights are business associates who require a BAA with the app company
options.B: Aggregate mental health trend data is not covered by the company's DPA since the DPA only governs raw user data
options.C: Using special-category health data to generate commercial insights sold to third parties requires a legal basis beyond what is needed for individual service delivery — and users likely did not consent to their health data being monetised for pharmaceutical market research
options.D: The outputs are not personal data so they can be shared without any restriction

items.question:
A hospital analytics team submits a pseudonymised patient dataset (no names, only age band and diagnosis category) to Claude for an analysis report. Claude's output includes: 'The only patient in the dataset who is aged 78–80, has a haematological malignancy, and received autologous stem cell transplant in Q1 is unique in the cohort — this case may warrant special review.' The team recognises this description likely identifies a specific patient from the hospital's records.

Which TWO actions should the team take in response? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The output is compliant since the input data was pseudonymised and no names appear in the output
options.B: Classify the output report as PHI and apply PHI-level access controls and handling before it is shared or stored
options.C: Request that Claude re-run the analysis with the unique-case flagging removed
options.D: Review and tighten the input minimisation controls to prevent field combinations that can narrow the cohort to a single individual in future analyses
options.E: No action is needed since the patient has not been named and the description alone cannot constitute a regulatory violation

items.question:
A strategy analyst at an investment bank prepares a research brief for submission to Claude by removing all client names and deal codes from the visible text and replacing them with generic placeholders. She uploads the source Word document, which was created collaboratively with annotations from four named colleagues. She considers the brief fully redacted before submission.

What critical step has the analyst omitted?

options.A: Metadata within the Word document — colleague names in tracked changes, comment attribution, and document-property fields — was not addressed and will be processed by Claude alongside the visible text
options.B: Generic placeholders must be tokenised before submission to prevent Claude from inferring the original client names
options.C: The document should have been submitted in JSON format rather than Word format to strip all metadata automatically
options.D: Colleague annotations are covered by internal employment agreements and pose no data risk when processed by an enterprise AI tool

items.question:
A UK healthcare company wants to transfer EU employee health data to a US-based Claude API endpoint on an ongoing, weekly basis. The legal team proposes relying on employee consent as both the lawful basis for processing and as the GDPR Article 49 derogation for the cross-border transfer. The DPO reviews the proposal and objects.

What is the MOST likely basis for the DPO's objection?

options.A: Employee consent is never a valid legal basis for processing health data under GDPR-style frameworks
options.B: Consent cannot be used as both the legal basis and the transfer mechanism simultaneously — a separate mechanism is required for each
options.C: The Article 49 derogation for consent is available only for occasional, non-repetitive transfers — systematic weekly transfers of employee health data cannot rely on consent as the transfer mechanism
options.D: EU employees cannot consent to cross-border transfers under GDPR because the power imbalance in employment relationships always renders consent involuntary

items.question:
A supply chain analyst at a pharmaceutical company bypasses the company's enterprise Claude account (which requires a 48-hour approval for new use cases) and uses a personal API key to run a time-sensitive vendor performance analysis. She submits a 15,000-row vendor dataset that includes vendor contact names, account manager emails, personal phone numbers, and commercially sensitive pricing data — all fields exported from the procurement system because it was faster than filtering the export.

Which statement MOST accurately characterises the combined governance failures in this scenario?

options.A: The analyst committed two independent governance failures: using an account without a DPA and audit logging for sensitive data, and submitting a dataset containing personal and commercially sensitive data far beyond what the vendor performance analysis required
options.B: The primary failure was using a personal account; the data scope is a secondary concern since vendor data is not personal data
options.C: The 48-hour approval process is the root cause of the failure and should be shortened so analysts use approved channels
options.D: The analyst's conduct was acceptable given the time-sensitive business context, provided the personal API key is registered with IT within 24 hours

items.question:
A hospital's Claude Project for surgical planning has been running for 26 months. The Project contains detailed patient case data from all completed surgeries. The hospital's retention schedule specifies 18 months for surgical planning records. Five clinicians who left the hospital between 6 and 18 months ago still have active Project logins — IT never revoked them. An internal audit has flagged both issues.

Which TWO governance actions are MOST overdue? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Immediately revoke the access of the five former clinicians to the Project
options.B: Archive the Project to read-only status to prevent further data additions while the issues are resolved
options.C: Delete surgical planning case data older than 18 months in accordance with the retention schedule
options.D: Upgrade the Project to a higher model tier to ensure the remaining data is analysed more accurately
options.E: Notify all patients whose case data is in the Project that their data has been retained beyond the scheduled period

items.question:
A workforce analytics lead at a 500-person financial services firm generates a dashboard showing employee survey results aggregated by team. Most teams have 15–30 members. However, two teams have 2 members each, and the dashboard shows their average satisfaction score, average tenure, and 'percentage who would recommend the firm as an employer.' The analytics lead considers the data safe to share since no names appear.

What is the PRIMARY risk the analytics lead has overlooked?

options.A: Two-person teams that submit different survey responses can be identified in aggregate since each member can calculate the other's response from the published average
options.B: An average of two values is a direct disclosure — members of a two-person team can determine each other's individual responses from the aggregate, making the published statistics individually identifying for those teams
options.C: Two-person teams are too small to provide statistically meaningful insights, so the data should be excluded on accuracy grounds rather than privacy grounds
options.D: The 'would recommend' percentage for a two-person team will always be 0%, 50%, or 100%, none of which is meaningful at team level

items.question:
An energy company's enterprise Claude DPA covers customer energy usage data for billing optimisation. The sustainability team wants to use the same account to process the same usage dataset combined with individual household income estimates (sourced from a third-party data broker) to identify households that qualify for a government energy efficiency subsidy. They have not involved the legal team.

What governance requirement must be satisfied BEFORE the sustainability team may proceed?

options.A: The energy company must obtain explicit consent from every customer before any energy usage data is processed
options.B: The DPA must be renegotiated at a higher service tier to accommodate the additional analytical complexity
options.C: The third-party income estimates must be encrypted before being combined with the usage data
options.D: The DPA must be amended to include the new data category (household income) and new processing purpose (subsidy qualification), and the legal basis for processing both datasets for this purpose must be established

items.question:
A mental health counselling practice employs three counsellors. Two use the practice's enterprise API account with a signed BAA. One part-time counsellor, not yet onboarded to the enterprise account, uses a personal Claude.ai subscription to document session notes containing client names, presenting concerns, diagnoses, and treatment approaches.

Which TWO statements MOST accurately describe the compliance failures created by this configuration? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Session notes are appropriate for AI processing only if clients have explicitly consented to AI use in their treatment — consent has not been mentioned in the scenario
options.B: Processing PHI through a personal consumer account without a BAA constitutes an unsanctioned disclosure of PHI to a non-business-associate channel, creating a HIPAA-style compliance failure
options.C: The practice cannot demonstrate consistent, auditable data-handling controls across all three counsellors, creating an accountability and documentation gap that cannot be remediated retroactively
options.D: The part-time status of the counsellor exempts them from the practice's data governance obligations since part-time staff are not covered entities
options.E: Session notes submitted to any AI tool automatically become part of the AI vendor's training dataset, making further use by the practice impossible

items.question:
A marketing team at a financial services firm uses a Claude Project for campaign analysis. The Project contains customer segment data including anonymised performance metrics and campaign response rates linked to demographic bands. The team lead who built and managed the Project left the firm six months ago. IT was not notified, so her enterprise account login was never revoked. An audit reveals she accessed the Project twice in the past month from an external network.

What is the MOST accurate description of the required immediate response?

options.A: The former team lead's access is low-risk since she no longer has a business motive and the data is customer segment aggregates rather than individual records
options.B: The Project should be deleted immediately to prevent any further unauthorized access to the data
options.C: Access should be revoked immediately, and the two unauthorized access events should be assessed as a potential data incident requiring investigation of what was viewed or extracted
options.D: The team should reset all Project passwords and inform the former team lead's previous clients that their data may have been accessed

items.question:
An HR technology lead at a 3,000-person regional bank is piloting Claude to screen CVs for an open credit analyst role. The model produces a ranked shortlist with scores and rationales for 420 applicants. A junior recruiter proposes using the AI-generated shortlist as the final hiring decision, skipping the interview panel to reduce time-to-hire by two weeks.

What is the MOST significant governance risk of adopting this proposal?

options.A: The bank removes the human decision-maker from a consequential employment decision, creating unmanaged accountability and bias-exposure gaps.
options.B: Claude's shortlist scores will conflict with the bank's applicant tracking system, causing data-integrity issues downstream.
options.C: Candidates excluded by the shortlist have no formal basis for appeal, exposing the bank to employment tribunal risk.
options.D: Bypassing interviews increases the likelihood that top-ranked candidates will accept competing offers before a contract is issued.

items.question:
A health-tech startup has deployed Claude in a patient-facing wellness app. Users describe symptoms and receive responses. During QA, a tester types: "I have had chest pain radiating to my left arm for the past hour." Claude replies with a ranked differential — musculoskeletal strain listed first as most probable — and suggests monitoring symptoms over the next 24 hours.

What is the PRIMARY governance concern with this response?

options.A: Claude's probability ranking has not been validated against a certified clinical diagnostic database, making the ordering statistically unreliable.
options.B: The response provides a substantive clinical assessment for a potentially life-threatening presentation without directing the user to seek emergency care.
options.C: Listing musculoskeletal strain first creates misleading health-claim liability under consumer product regulations.
options.D: The response is too detailed; wellness apps should cap AI output at three sentences to avoid overwhelming users with clinical terminology.

items.question:
A consumer lending company uses Claude to draft adverse-action letters sent to loan applicants who are declined. A compliance officer reviews each letter before it is mailed and notices they contain no mention of AI involvement. She asks the operations director whether a disclosure is necessary.

What is the BEST governance response to the compliance officer's concern?

options.A: No disclosure is needed because the compliance officer reviewed and approved each letter, making the human the author of record.
options.B: Disclosure is only required if the AI directly made the credit decision, not if it only drafted the letter explaining the decision.
options.C: Consequential communications informing individuals of adverse decisions warrant disclosure of AI involvement as a transparency obligation, even when the AI role was limited to drafting.
options.D: The legal team should determine whether current regulations compel disclosure before any language is added to the letters.

items.question:
A property insurer uses an AI tool to flag claims exhibiting fraud-associated patterns. When the tool flags a claim, a claims manager receives a notification and is expected to review the file before approving the determination. Over six months, the manager approved every AI flag as a valid fraud finding without opening any claim files, citing the tool's high historical accuracy rate. One flagged claim turns out to be legitimate; the policyholder's home repairs were delayed four months while the claim was frozen.

Who bears PRIMARY accountability for the outcome?

options.A: The AI vendor, because the tool's false-positive rate was not adequately disclosed in the service agreement.
options.B: The policyholder, because submitting a claim that closely matched fraud patterns contributed to the processing delay.
options.C: The insurer's IT department, because they deployed the tool without sufficient validation testing for the insurer's specific claims portfolio.
options.D: The claims manager, because they held decision-making authority and failed to exercise genuine judgment when reviewing flagged claims.

items.question:
A fintech startup offering small business loans proposes a fully automated lending pipeline: Claude analyses the application and supporting financial documents, produces a credit assessment, and the system sends an approval or denial email to the applicant with no human review. The CTO's rationale is speed — most applicants receive a response within minutes.

What is the MOST appropriate governance response to this proposal?

options.A: Require a qualified human to review and authorise the credit decision before any approval or denial is communicated to the applicant.
options.B: Implement a dollar threshold so that only loans below a set amount are fully automated, while larger amounts require human review.
options.C: Add an explanation of the decision criteria to denial emails so that applicants understand why they were declined.
options.D: Run a six-month accuracy pilot to validate the model's performance before removing human review from the pipeline.

items.question:
A 90,000-person technology enterprise uses Claude to generate first-draft performance ratings for 12,000 employees based on project records, peer feedback, and manager notes. An internal audit finds that employees in one geographic region consistently receive lower AI-generated draft ratings than peers with equivalent documented outputs. HR leadership argues that manager adjustments before final submission mean the bias in the drafts does not affect final ratings.

Why is HR leadership's position MOST likely incorrect?

options.A: Manager adjustments are not statistically validated, so there is no evidence they correct the draft bias rather than compounding it.
options.B: Anchoring effects mean managers are likely to adjust ratings toward, rather than away from, the AI-generated draft, so regional bias persists into final ratings.
options.C: The audit finding creates a legal disclosure obligation to affected employees that must be satisfied before the ratings cycle closes.
options.D: Draft ratings stored in the HR system become part of the permanent record, causing biased values to propagate even after final adjustments are made.

items.question:
A 400-person logistics company runs an anonymous employee engagement survey. HR uses Claude to analyse the 380 responses and produce a themes report for the executive team. Six months later, an employee asks HR whether AI was used to process the survey data. The HR director replies that because the survey was anonymous, no consent or notice for AI analysis was needed.

What is the MOST accurate assessment of the HR director's position?

options.A: The position is correct — anonymisation removes personal data from the scope of consent obligations, so no notice was required.
options.B: The position is partially correct — no notice was needed before the survey, but the company should have disclosed AI use in follow-up employee communications.
options.C: The position is incorrect — even for anonymised datasets, employees have a reasonable expectation of notice when AI is used to analyse data they contributed, and the disclosure should have appeared in the survey introduction.
options.D: The position is incorrect — the survey should have excluded free-text fields before AI analysis, because open responses can re-identify individuals despite anonymisation.

items.question:
A solo management consultant uses Claude to help draft client deliverables. A client whose employment contract was terminated early asks the consultant to produce a legal opinion letter on whether the termination was wrongful and what remedies are available. The consultant uses Claude to generate the letter and plans to send it on their own firm's letterhead with no disclaimer.

What is the MOST significant risk of proceeding as planned?

options.A: Claude may generate a letter that is too long for the client to act on without further professional guidance.
options.B: The letterhead may confuse the client about the professional credentials of the person providing the advice.
options.C: Claude's training data may not reflect current employment law in the client's jurisdiction, making the legal analysis unreliable.
options.D: Issuing a legal opinion letter without being a qualified legal professional constitutes practising law, for which the consultant has no licence, regardless of how the letter was drafted.

items.question:
A junior analyst at a 12-person independent wealth management firm uses Claude to help draft client communications. A long-standing client emails asking whether to rebalance their equity portfolio given current market volatility, and what specific bond allocation percentage the analyst recommends. The analyst asks Claude to generate a specific allocation recommendation and pastes it into a reply email.

What is the MOST appropriate course of action instead?

options.A: Refer the client's specific question to a licensed investment adviser within the firm before providing any recommendation.
options.B: Include a disclaimer in the email stating the recommendation is AI-generated and should be treated as informational only.
options.C: Use Claude to draft the recommendation but have the junior analyst personally review it for accuracy before sending.
options.D: Send the recommendation as drafted, because the firm's professional indemnity insurance covers advice given in good faith on behalf of clients.

items.question:
A national retail chain uses Claude to analyse attendance records, CCTV logs, and manager incident reports to produce disciplinary recommendation reports. An operations manager receives a Claude-generated report recommending a final written warning for an employee with three recorded absences. The manager signs the formal warning letter and files it in the HR system without reading the underlying incident reports or speaking with the employee.

What is the PRIMARY governance failure in this scenario?

options.A: The operations manager did not consult the HR department before issuing a formal warning, bypassing the required escalation path.
options.B: The disciplinary decision was effectively made by the AI tool; the manager's signature provided administrative form without genuine human deliberation.
options.C: CCTV data should not be used as an input for disciplinary analysis without explicit employee consent at the point of capture.
options.D: Claude's output was not reviewed by a second manager before action was taken, violating the four-eyes principle required for disciplinary decisions.

items.question:
A hospital emergency department has deployed a validated AI triage tool that assigns patients an acuity score from 1 (immediate) to 5 (non-urgent). The tool is highly accurate on average. During a busy overnight shift, a triage nurse follows the AI score exclusively for eight consecutive patients without applying independent clinical assessment in order to manage queue length. One patient scored 4 is later found to be in early septic shock and experiences a serious adverse outcome.

Which statement BEST characterises the governance failure?

options.A: The tool was not calibrated for overnight patient populations, which have different acuity distributions than daytime cohorts the model was validated on.
options.B: The hospital's staffing model created structurally unmanageable queue pressure, making it impossible for the nurse to perform independent assessments within shift constraints.
options.C: The nurse used the AI score as a substitute for clinical judgment rather than a data point within it, nullifying the human oversight the workflow was designed to provide.
options.D: The acuity scoring range was too coarse — a five-point scale cannot capture sufficient clinical nuance to safely support emergency triage.

items.question:
A chemical manufacturer uses Claude to monitor sensor data from a production line and flag anomalies. When the system flags a temperature spike suggesting a potential runaway reaction, it sends an automated shutdown command to the line without waiting for engineer confirmation. An engineer on shift later determines the spike was a faulty sensor reading; no hazard was present, and the unplanned shutdown cost four hours of production and a significant batch loss.

What does this scenario PRIMARILY illustrate about AI in safety-critical environments?

options.A: AI monitoring tools should not be used in chemical manufacturing until industry-wide sensor reliability standards are higher.
options.B: The cost of the unplanned shutdown demonstrates that AI automation is not yet cost-effective for manufacturing safety applications.
options.C: The AI system should be retrained on historical sensor-failure data so it can distinguish faulty readings from genuine anomalies.
options.D: Safety-critical automated actions with significant operational consequences require a human confirmation step before execution, not only a flag for later review.

items.question:
A senior consultant at a professional services firm uses the company's Claude enterprise deployment during a late evening to draft a detailed letter disputing a personal dispute with their landlord over a security deposit. The firm's IT team discovers this in aggregated usage logs and flags it for the HR director.

What is the PRIMARY acceptable-use concern this incident illustrates?

options.A: The consultant used a company AI resource for personal legal purposes outside the permitted scope of workplace use, which the firm's acceptable-use policy should address.
options.B: Claude may have provided legally inaccurate advice about landlord-tenant law, exposing the consultant to harm from acting on incorrect information.
options.C: The usage logs containing details of the consultant's personal dispute create a data retention and privacy obligation the firm did not anticipate.
options.D: The firm's Claude subscription may not include authorised use for legal-domain queries, potentially violating the vendor's terms of service.

items.question:
A city council's planning department submits an AI-generated analysis of housing demand projections to a full council meeting as part of a major rezoning decision. The 28-page report is attributed to the department's data analytics team; there is no mention that Claude was used to synthesise and interpret the underlying data. A councillor later asks the analytics lead how the analysis was produced.

What is the MOST significant governance concern this situation raises?

options.A: The council has no approved AI technology procurement on record for Claude, making the department's use potentially unsanctioned.
options.B: Council members voted on a consequential public decision without knowing that AI was materially involved in the analysis they relied upon, limiting their ability to appropriately scrutinise it.
options.C: Claude's housing demand projections may not be accurate, because the model's training data predates current planning regulations in this jurisdiction.
options.D: Attributing the report to the analytics team without individual author names creates an accountability gap in the event the analysis is later found to be flawed.

items.question:
A health insurer's claims adjuster uses Claude to evaluate a complex out-of-network claim. Based on the adjuster's brief description of policy terms, Claude produces a coverage interpretation recommending denial. The adjuster copies the recommendation verbatim into the denial letter and sends it without independent review. The policyholder appeals; an external review board finds the denial was incorrect — the coverage interpretation Claude applied did not reflect the most recent policy amendment. A regulator asks the insurer to identify who is accountable for the incorrect denial.

Who bears PRIMARY accountability?

options.A: The AI vendor, because the tool's coverage knowledge was not current and this was not disclosed in the product documentation.
options.B: The insurer's legal team, because they failed to provide the adjuster with updated policy documentation to input into the AI tool.
options.C: The claims adjuster, because they held decision-making authority and issued a denial based on AI output they did not independently verify.
options.D: The policyholder, because selecting an out-of-network provider created a foreseeable coverage ambiguity that required complex interpretation.
